claim: Pentameric ligand-gated ion channels (pLGICs) mediate fast chemical signaling through global allosteric transitions.
source: Pentameric ligand-gated ion channels (pLGICs) mediate fast chemical signaling through global allosteric transitions.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about pLGICs function.

claim: Proton application causes a global compaction of the extracellular subunit interface in GLIC.
source: We show that proton application causes a global compaction of the extracellular subunit interface, coupled to an outward motion of the M2-M3 loop near the channel gate.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence quenching data from multiple bimane-labeled mutants showing decreased fluorescence upon acidification.

claim: Proton application causes an outward motion of the M2-M3 loop near the channel gate in GLIC.
source: We show that proton application causes a global compaction of the extracellular subunit interface, coupled to an outward motion of the M2-M3 loop near the channel gate.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence data from the Bimane-250-Y197 pair showing increased fluorescence upon acidification.

claim: The conformational reorganizations in GLIC are highly similar in lipid vesicles and detergent micelles.
source: These movements are highly similar in lipid vesicles and detergent micelles.
evidence: This is supported by steady-state fluorescence measurements comparing detergent and liposome conditions shown in Figure 5 and Table 3.

claim: The conformational reorganizations in GLIC are essentially completed within 2 ms.
source: These reorganizations are essentially completed within 2 ms and occur without channel opening at low proton concentration, indicating that they report a pre-active intermediate state in the transition pathway toward activation.
evidence: This is supported by stopped-flow fluorescence measurements showing that the majority of fluorescence changes occur in the dead-time of the instrument (Figure 6 and Table 5).

claim: The conformational reorganizations in GLIC occur without channel opening at low proton concentration.
source: These reorganizations are essentially completed within 2 ms and occur without channel opening at low proton concentration, indicating that they report a pre-active intermediate state in the transition pathway toward activation.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of fluorescence changes and ion flux measurements showing that fluorescence changes occur at pH values where no channel activity is detected (Figure 7A).

claim: The conformational reorganizations report a pre-active intermediate state in the transition pathway toward activation.
source: These reorganizations are essentially completed within 2 ms and occur without channel opening at low proton concentration, indicating that they report a pre-active intermediate state in the transition pathway toward activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that conformational changes occur before channel opening, as shown by the separation between fluorescence and ion flux pH-response curves.

claim: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) are prominent members of the pLGIC family.
source: Prominent members of the family include nicotinic acetylcholine (nAChRs), serotonin-type-3 (5-HT3Rs), glycine (GlyRs) and γ-aminobutyric acid-A (GABAARs) receptors that are widely expressed in the nervous system.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the pLGIC family.

claim: Serotonin-type-3 receptors (5-HT3Rs) are prominent members of the pLGIC family.
source: Prominent members of the family include nicotinic acetylcholine (nAChRs), serotonin-type-3 (5-HT3Rs), glycine (GlyRs) and γ-aminobutyric acid-A (GABAARs) receptors that are widely expressed in the nervous system.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the pLGIC family.

claim: Glycine receptors (GlyRs) are prominent members of the pLGIC family.
source: Prominent members of the family include nicotinic acetylcholine (nAChRs), serotonin-type-3 (5-HT3Rs), glycine (GlyRs) and γ-aminobutyric acid-A (GABAARs) receptors that are widely expressed in the nervous system.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the pLGIC family.

claim: γ-aminobutyric acid-A receptors (GABAARs) are prominent members of the pLGIC family.
source: Prominent members of the family include nicotinic acetylcholine (nAChRs), serotonin-type-3 (5-HT3Rs), glycine (GlyRs) and γ-aminobutyric acid-A (GABAARs) receptors that are widely expressed in the nervous system.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the pLGIC family.

claim: Mutations in pLGICs can cause congenital myasthenia.
source: Their mutation can cause congenital myasthenia, epilepsy, hyperekplexia and possibly autistic and schizophrenic syndromes (Steinlein, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Steinlein, 2012.

claim: Mutations in pLGICs can cause epilepsy.
source: Their mutation can cause congenital myasthenia, epilepsy, hyperekplexia and possibly autistic and schizophrenic syndromes (Steinlein, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Steinlein, 2012.

claim: Mutations in pLGICs can cause hyperekplexia.
source: Their mutation can cause congenital myasthenia, epilepsy, hyperekplexia and possibly autistic and schizophrenic syndromes (Steinlein, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Steinlein, 2012.

claim: Mutations in pLGICs possibly cause autistic syndromes.
source: Their mutation can cause congenital myasthenia, epilepsy, hyperekplexia and possibly autistic and schizophrenic syndromes (Steinlein, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Steinlein, 2012, with the qualifier 'possibly' indicating speculation.

claim: Mutations in pLGICs possibly cause schizophrenic syndromes.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Steinlein, 2012, with the qualifier 'possibly' indicating speculation.

claim: pLGICs are the target of anxiolytics and sedatives.
source: They are the target of major classes of therapeutic substances, including anxiolytics and sedatives, general anesthetics, smoking cessation drugs and antiemetics (Corringer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Corringer et al., 2012.

claim: pLGICs are the target of general anesthetics.
source: They are the target of major classes of therapeutic substances, including anxiolytics and sedatives, general anesthetics, smoking cessation drugs and antiemetics (Corringer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Corringer et al., 2012.

claim: pLGICs are the target of smoking cessation drugs.
source: They are the target of major classes of therapeutic substances, including anxiolytics and sedatives, general anesthetics, smoking cessation drugs and antiemetics (Corringer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Corringer et al., 2012.

claim: pLGICs are the target of antiemetics.
source: They are the target of major classes of therapeutic substances, including anxiolytics and sedatives, general anesthetics, smoking cessation drugs and antiemetics (Corringer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Corringer et al., 2012.

claim: The first X-ray structure of a full-length pLGIC was obtained on the bacterial homolog ELIC.
source: the first X-ray structures of full-length pLGICs were obtained on the bacterial homologs Erwinia chrysanthemi Ligand-gated Ion Channel (ELIC) (Hilf and Dutzler, 2008) and Gloeobacter violaceus Ligand-gated Ion Channel (GLIC) (Bocquet et al., 2009; Hilf and Dutzler, 2009; Sauguet et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hilf and Dutzler, 2008.

claim: The first X-ray structure of a full-length pLGIC was obtained on the bacterial homolog GLIC.
source: the first X-ray structures of full-length pLGICs were obtained on the bacterial homologs Erwinia chrysanthemi Ligand-gated Ion Channel (ELIC) (Hilf and Dutzler, 2008) and Gloeobacter violaceus Ligand-gated Ion Channel (GLIC) (Bocquet et al., 2009; Hilf and Dutzler, 2009; Sauguet et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bocquet et al., 2009; Hilf and Dutzler, 2009; Sauguet et al., 2014.

claim: pLGICs are composed of five identical or homologous subunits arranged pseudosymmetrically around a central ion-conducting channel.
source: pLGICs are composed of five identical or homologous subunits arranged pseudosymmetrically around a central ion-conducting channel.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about pLGICs.

claim: pLGICs bind neurotransmitters within their extracellular domain (ECD).
source: They bind neurotransmitters within their extracellular domain (ECD), promoting remote opening of an intrinsic ion channel within their transmembrane domain (TMD).
evidence: This is established structural and functional knowledge about pLGICs.

claim: Neurotransmitter binding to the ECD promotes opening of an ion channel within the transmembrane domain (TMD) of pLGICs.
source: They bind neurotransmitters within their extracellular domain (ECD), promoting remote opening of an intrinsic ion channel within their transmembrane domain (TMD).
evidence: This is established structural and functional knowledge about pLGICs.

claim: The orthosteric binding sites for neurotransmitters in pLGICs are located at the subunit interface.
source: The orthosteric binding sites for neurotransmitters are located at the subunit interface, halfway between the membrane and the top of the ECD.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about pLGICs.

claim: M2 lines the ion channel in pLGICs.
source: M2 lines the ion channel, its upper part contributing to the gate that shuts the pore in the closed conformation.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about pLGICs.

claim: The upper part of M2 contributes to the gate that shuts the pore in the closed conformation of pLGICs.
source: M2 lines the ion channel, its upper part contributing to the gate that shuts the pore in the closed conformation.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about pLGICs.

claim: pLGICs exist in multiple allosteric states including resting, active, and desensitized states.
source: The major states can be classified as: resting (with a closed channel and a low affinity for agonists), active (with an open channel) and desensitized (with a closed channel and a high affinity for agonists) (Changeux and Edelstein, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Changeux and Edelstein, 2005.

claim: The resting state of pLGICs has a closed channel and a low affinity for agonists.
source: The major states can be classified as: resting (with a closed channel and a low affinity for agonists), active (with an open channel) and desensitized (with a closed channel and a high affinity for agonists) (Changeux and Edelstein, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Changeux and Edelstein, 2005.

claim: The active state of pLGICs has an open channel.
source: The major states can be classified as: resting (with a closed channel and a low affinity for agonists), active (with an open channel) and desensitized (with a closed channel and a high affinity for agonists) (Changeux and Edelstein, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Changeux and Edelstein, 2005.

claim: The desensitized state of pLGICs has a closed channel and a high affinity for agonists.
source: The major states can be classified as: resting (with a closed channel and a low affinity for agonists), active (with an open channel) and desensitized (with a closed channel and a high affinity for agonists) (Changeux and Edelstein, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Changeux and Edelstein, 2005.

claim: Ensemble and single-channel kinetic analyses identified short-lived intermediate states during activation of nAChRs and GlyRs.
source: In addition, ensemble and single-channel kinetic analyses identified short-lived intermediate states during activation of nAChRs and GlyRs. These states, named 'flip' and 'prime', display increased agonist affinity as compared to the resting state but still carry a closed channel (Burzomato et al., 2004; Lape et al., 2008; Mukhtasimova et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burzomato et al., 2004; Lape et al., 2008; Mukhtasimova et al., 2009.

claim: The 'flip' and 'prime' intermediate states display increased agonist affinity compared to the resting state but still carry a closed channel.
source: These states, named 'flip' and 'prime', display increased agonist affinity as compared to the resting state but still carry a closed channel (Burzomato et al., 2004; Lape et al., 2008; Mukhtasimova et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burzomato et al., 2004; Lape et al., 2008; Mukhtasimova et al., 2009.

claim: Desensitization involves multiple conformations, including fast and slow desensitized states.
source: Finally, desensitization was early described as involving multiple conformations, including fast and slow desensitized states (Sakmann et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sakmann et al., 1980.

claim: GLIC was solved in three different conformations.
source: GLIC has been crystallized in three conformations (called open, closed and locally-closed) (Bocquet et al., 2009; Prevost et al., 2012; Sauguet et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bocquet et al., 2009; Prevost et al., 2012; Sauguet et al., 2014.

claim: The three conformations of GLIC are called open, closed and locally-closed.
source: GLIC has been crystallized in three conformations (called open, closed and locally-closed) (Bocquet et al., 2009; Prevost et al., 2012; Sauguet et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bocquet et al., 2009; Prevost et al., 2012; Sauguet et al., 2014.

claim: The TrIQ method consists in covalently linking the protein with a fluorophore together with the insertion of a tryptophan residue that quenches the fluorophore when the inter-residue Cα-Cα distances are less than approximately 15 Å.
source: The methods consist in covalently linking the protein with a fluorophore, here the small and pH-insensitive bimane (Figure 2A), together with the insertion of a tryptophan or a tyrosine residue that quenches the fluorophore when the inter-residue Cα-Cα distances are less than approximately 15 Å and 10 Å, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of the TrIQ method used in the study.

claim: The TyrIQ method consists in covalently linking the protein with a fluorophore together with the insertion of a tyrosine residue that quenches the fluorophore when the inter-residue Cα-Cα distances are less than approximately 10 Å.
source: The methods consist in covalently linking the protein with a fluorophore, here the small and pH-insensitive bimane (Figure 2A), together with the insertion of a tryptophan or a tyrosine residue that quenches the fluorophore when the inter-residue Cα-Cα distances are less than approximately 15 Å and 10 Å, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of the TyrIQ method used in the study.

claim: The TrIQ approach was validated on the model system T4 lysosyme.
source: The Tr/TyrIQ approach was validated on the model system T4 lysosyme (Mansoor et al., 2002, 2010; Jones Brunette et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mansoor et al., 2002, 2010; Jones Brunette et al., 2014.

claim: The TrIQ method was previously used to follow the allosteric transitions of the β2-adrenoceptor.
source: and was previously used to follow the allosteric transitions of proteins such as the β2-adrenoceptor (Yao et al., 2006) and the lactose permease (Smirnova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yao et al., 2006.

claim: The TrIQ method was previously used to follow the allosteric transitions of the lactose permease.
source: and was previously used to follow the allosteric transitions of proteins such as the β2-adrenoceptor (Yao et al., 2006) and the lactose permease (Smirnova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smirnova et al., 2014.

claim: Bimane is small and pH-insensitive.
source: The methods consist in covalently linking the protein with a fluorophore, here the small and pH-insensitive bimane (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is a characterization of the bimane fluorophore used in the study.

claim: Both the bimane fluorescence and its quenching by tryptophans are unaffected by proton concentrations ranging from pH 9 to pH 2.
source: GLIC being activated by protons, we additionally performed control experiments to confirm that, as previous studies have shown (Jones Brunette et al., 2014), both the bimane fluorescence and its quenching by tryptophans are unaffected by proton concentrations ranging from pH 9 to pH 2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B and citation to Jones Brunette et al., 2014.

claim: Bimane-133 shows a marked blue shift (15 nm) at pH 7.3.
source: Bimane-133 shows a marked blue shift (15 nm) and a fluorescence two times higher than the denatured protein at pH 7.3 possibly indicating the probe when reacted to position 133 is located in a confined/hydrophobic environment (Kosower et al., 1982; Skjold-Jørgensen et al., 2015) (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Bimane-133 shows a fluorescence two times higher than the denatured protein at pH 7.3.
source: Bimane-133 shows a marked blue shift (15 nm) and a fluorescence two times higher than the denatured protein at pH 7.3 possibly indicating the probe when reacted to position 133 is located in a confined/hydrophobic environment (Kosower et al., 1982; Skjold-Jørgensen et al., 2015) (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The probe at position 133 is possibly located in a confined/hydrophobic environment.
source: Bimane-133 shows a marked blue shift (15 nm) and a fluorescence two times higher than the denatured protein at pH 7.3 possibly indicating the probe when reacted to position 133 is located in a confined/hydrophobic environment (Kosower et al., 1982; Skjold-Jørgensen et al., 2015) (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the blue shift and increased fluorescence, supported by citations to Kosower et al., 1982; Skjold-Jørgensen et al., 2015.

claim: Bimane-133-W103 shows a marked pH-dependent fluorescence decrease.
source: In contrast, both the Bimane-133-W103 and Bimane-136-W101 show a marked pH-dependent fluorescence decrease (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Bimane-136-W101 shows a marked pH-dependent fluorescence decrease.
source: In contrast, both the Bimane-133-W103 and Bimane-136-W101 show a marked pH-dependent fluorescence decrease (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Residues at positions 133 and 103 come closer together upon acidification of GLIC.
source: These data show that the residues at positions 133 and 103, and those at positions 136 and 101 come closer upon acidification of the receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the pH-dependent fluorescence decrease of Bimane-133-W103.

claim: Residues at positions 136 and 101 come closer together upon acidification of GLIC.
source: These data show that the residues at positions 133 and 103, and those at positions 136 and 101 come closer upon acidification of the receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the pH-dependent fluorescence decrease of Bimane-136-W101.

claim: The X-ray structure of Bimane-135 GLIC at pH 4 was solved at 2.6 Å resolution.
source: To determine whether W72 has a role in the fluorescence phenotype while avoiding severe mutation-induced structural alteration that would result from the loss of W72, we solved the X-ray structure of Bimane-135 GLIC at pH 4 at 2.6 Å resolution (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the crystallographic data presented in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: The structure of Bimane-135 GLIC shows a protein conformation quasi-identical to the wild-type GLIC structure at pH 4 (RMSD = 0.26 Å).
source: The structure shows a protein conformation quasi-identical to the wild-type GLIC structure (Bocquet et al., 2009) at pH 4 (RMSD = 0.26 Å)
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data and citation to Bocquet et al., 2009.

claim: The bimane at position 135 is at a minimal 3.2 Å distance from the indole ring of W72.
source: The data indeed show that the bimane is at a minimal 3.2 Å distance from the indole ring of W72, which is therefore most likely the major partner in the pH-elicited fluorescence changes of Bimane-135 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: W72 is most likely the major partner in the pH-elicited fluorescence changes of Bimane-135.
source: The data indeed show that the bimane is at a minimal 3.2 Å distance from the indole ring of W72, which is therefore most likely the major partner in the pH-elicited fluorescence changes of Bimane-135 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the close distance between the bimane and W72 in the crystal structure.

claim: The quenching of Bimane-135 by W72 seen up to pH 4 suggests a contraction of the domains interfaces.
source: As the 135 side chain projects at the subunit interface, the quenching of Bimane-135 by W72 seen up to pH 4 suggests a contraction of the domains interfaces, driving the bimane moiety toward W72, although other mechanisms are possible.
evidence: This is inferred from the fluorescence quenching data and structural information.

claim: Bimane-33 shows a twofold pH-dependent decrease in fluorescence from pH 7.3 to pH 5.
source: Bimane-33 shows a twofold pH-dependent decrease in fluorescence from pH 7.3 to pH 5 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: W160F mutation essentially abolishes the proton-elicited fluorescent decrease of Bimane-33.
source: Its mutation (W160F) essentially abolishes the proton-elicited fluorescent decrease, with only a 20% decrease in intensity at pH 6, followed by a return to pH 7-like values at lower pHs, showing that Bimane-33 and W160 come closer together in the presence of protons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing Bimane-33-W160 and Bimane-33-W160F.

claim: Bimane-33 and W160 come closer together in the presence of protons.
source: Its mutation (W160F) essentially abolishes the proton-elicited fluorescent decrease, with only a 20% decrease in intensity at pH 6, followed by a return to pH 7-like values at lower pHs, showing that Bimane-33 and W160 come closer together in the presence of protons.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of the W160F mutation on fluorescence.

claim: Bimane-250 shows a 30% increase in intensity as the pH is decreased from 7.3 to 3.
source: Bimane-250 shows a 30% increase in intensity as the pH is decreased from 7.3 to 3 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Positions 250 and 197 move away from each other in the presence of protons.
source: In contrast, the mutant Bimane-250-Y197F is functional, the unquenching phenotype showing that positions 250 and 197 move away from each other in the presence of protons (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is inferred from the unquenching phenotype of Bimane-250-Y197F.

claim: Bimane-243 shows an emission blue shift (10 nm) at pH 7.3.
source: In addition, the mutant Bimane-243 shows an emission blue shift (10 nm) and a fluorescence 1.6 times higher than the denatured protein at pH 7.3 possibly reporting a confined/hydrophobic environment of the probe (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Bimane-243 shows a fluorescence 1.6 times higher than the denatured protein at pH 7.3.
source: In addition, the mutant Bimane-243 shows an emission blue shift (10 nm) and a fluorescence 1.6 times higher than the denatured protein at pH 7.3 possibly reporting a confined/hydrophobic environment of the probe (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The bimane at position 243 possibly reports a confined/hydrophobic environment.
source: In addition, the mutant Bimane-243 shows an emission blue shift (10 nm) and a fluorescence 1.6 times higher than the denatured protein at pH 7.3 possibly reporting a confined/hydrophobic environment of the probe (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is inferred from the blue shift and increased fluorescence.

claim: The mutant Bimane-135-W72-E67Q-E75Q-D91N shows the same pH-dependence of fluorescence as the simple mutant Bimane-135-W72.
source: This mutant shows the same pH-dependence of fluorescence as the simple mutant Bimane-135-W72 (Figure 4A), supporting the hypothesis that the fluorescence variations are independent of the protonation of surrounding titratable residues.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The fluorescence variations of Bimane-135-W72 are independent of the protonation of surrounding titratable residues.
source: This mutant shows the same pH-dependence of fluorescence as the simple mutant Bimane-135-W72 (Figure 4A), supporting the hypothesis that the fluorescence variations are independent of the protonation of surrounding titratable residues.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Bimane-135-W72 and Bimane-135-W72-E67Q-E75Q-D91N.

claim: Propofol binds to the transmembrane domain of GLIC with an IC50 ≈ 25 µM.
source: Propofol binds to the transmembrane domain of GLIC with an IC50 ≈ 25 µM and stabilizes closed channel conformations (Nury et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nury et al., 2011.

claim: Propofol stabilizes closed channel conformations of GLIC.
source: Propofol binds to the transmembrane domain of GLIC with an IC50 ≈ 25 µM and stabilizes closed channel conformations (Nury et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nury et al., 2011.

claim: In presence of saturating concentrations of propofol, mutants Bimane-136-W101, Bimane-135-W72, Bimane-250-Y197 and Bimane-243 show a shift of the pH-fluorescence relationship curve toward higher proton concentrations.
source: In presence of saturating concentrations of propofol, mutants Bimane-136-W101, Bimane-135-W72, Bimane-250-Y197 and Bimane-243 show a shift of the pH-fluorescence relationship curve toward higher proton concentrations, in agreement with the effect of an allosteric inhibitor (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The binding of propofol to the TMD influences the fluorescence variations at the top of the ECD, more than 50 Å away.
source: The observation that the binding of an effector to the TMD influences the fluorescence variations at the top of the ECD, more than 50 Å away, establishes that the fluorescence sensors indeed report global allosteric motions.
evidence: This is inferred from the propofol effect on fluorescence at distant sites.

claim: The fluorescence sensors report global allosteric motions.
source: The observation that the binding of an effector to the TMD influences the fluorescence variations at the top of the ECD, more than 50 Å away, establishes that the fluorescence sensors indeed report global allosteric motions.
evidence: This is inferred from the long-range effect of propofol on fluorescence.

claim: At the top and middle of the ECD, steady-state fluorescence variations are similar in detergent micelles and liposomes.
source: Strikingly, at the top and middle of the ECD (Bimane-133 ± W103, Bimane-135-W72 and Bimane-136 ± W101), steady-state fluorescence variations are similar, if not identical, in detergent micelles and liposomes (Figure 5A,B,C, Table 1 and Table 3)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B,C, Table 1 and Table 3.

claim: The movements at the top and middle of the ECD are independent of the membrane environment.
source: Strikingly, at the top and middle of the ECD (Bimane-133 ± W103, Bimane-135-W72 and Bimane-136 ± W101), steady-state fluorescence variations are similar, if not identical, in detergent micelles and liposomes (Figure 5A,B,C, Table 1 and Table 3), indicating that the corresponding movements are independent of the membrane environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of fluorescence variations in different membrane environments.

claim: Liposome reconstitution causes a significant increase in fluorescence of Bimane-33 and Bimane-250-Y197F mutants at pH 8/7, as compared to detergent conditions.
source: At the ECD-TMD interface, liposome reconstitution causes a significant increase in fluorescence of Bimane-33 and Bimane-250-Y197F mutants at pH 8/7, as compared to detergent conditions (30% and 50%, respectively) (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 3.

claim: The marked pH-dependent changes of Bimane-250 and Bimane-33 are conserved in lipids.
source: To better visualize the pH-dependent changes, the data were normalized to the pH 8/7 values, showing that the marked pH-dependent changes of Bimane-250 and Bimane-33 are conserved in lipids, although Bimane-33-W160F is significantly brighter in detergent (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: Bimane-243 shows similar pH-dependent variations in fluorescence in detergent and lipids.
source: Additionally, Bimane-243 shows similar pH-dependent variations in fluorescence in detergent and lipids (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The relative movements at positions 33–160 and 250–197 are essentially conserved in lipids.
source: The data thus suggest that the relative movements at positions 33–160 and 250–197 are also essentially conserved in lipids.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of pH-dependent fluorescence changes in lipids.

claim: GLIC retains the ability to undergo proton-elicited conformational change and to activate in PC liposomes and other lipid mixtures.
source: GLIC does not exhibit the same propensity to adopt an uncoupled conformation and, contrary to ELIC, retains the ability to undergo proton-elicited conformational change and to activate in PC liposomes and other lipid mixtures (Labriola et al., 2013; Velisetty and Chakrapani, 2012; Dellisanti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Labriola et al., 2013; Velisetty and Chakrapani, 2012; Dellisanti et al., 2013.

claim: A cluster of Trp residues strengthening M4 interactions with M1/M3 critically contributes to the robustness of GLIC function in various lipid environments.
source: A cluster of Trp residues, strengthening M4 interactions with M1/M3, was found to critically contribute to this robustness of GLIC function in various lipid environments (Hénault et al., 2015; Carswell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hénault et al., 2015; Carswell et al., 2015.

claim: For most positions, the changes in fluorescence are found to mainly occur in the dead-time of the instrument, during the first 2 ms of solution mixing.
source: For most positions, the changes in fluorescence (as compared to the fluorescence at pH 8) are found to mainly occur in the dead-time of the instrument, during the first 2 ms of solution mixing (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by stopped-flow fluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Completion of the fluorescence variations in 2 ms indicates an upper value of the time constant below 1 ms.
source: While this very fast component is not resolved here, completion of the fluorescence variations in 2 ms indicates an upper value of the time constant below 1 ms.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic analysis of the stopped-flow data.

claim: At positions 133, 136, 33 and 250, the dead-time 2 ms component accounts for the majority of the fluorescence variation.
source: At positions 133, 136, 33 and 250, the dead-time 2 ms ('very fast') component, evaluated at the start of the multi-exponential fit at 5 ms, accounts for the majority of the fluorescence variation, especially at pH 4 where 72% to 90% of the fluorescence changes are completed (Figure 6C and Table 5).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 6C and Table 5.

claim: The motion of positions 136–101, 133–103 and 33–160 moving closer together, and the separation of 250–197 occur with very fast kinetics.
source: Therefore, the motion of positions 136–101, 133–103 and 33–160 moving closer together, and the separation of 250–197 occur with very fast kinetics.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic analysis showing that most fluorescence changes occur within 2 ms.

claim: Bimane-243 shows a distinctive kinetic pattern with its very fast component accounting for only 40% of the fluorescence variation.
source: Interestingly, Bimane-243 shows a distinctive kinetic pattern, as its very fast component accounts for only 40% of the fluorescence variation. This is followed by fast and intermediate components accounting for 30% and 20% of the fluorescence variation, respectively (Figure 6C and Table 5).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 6C and Table 5.

claim: The upper part of the channel moves over a broad time scale.
source: Although the fluorescence changes at position 243 could not be assigned to particular conformational motions, these data suggest that the upper part of the channel moves over a broad time scale.
evidence: This is inferred from the distinctive kinetic pattern of Bimane-243.

claim: Slow components of fluorescence variations were recorded with time constants ranging from 1 to 30 s at all positions.
source: Finally, at all positions, slow components of fluorescence variations were recorded with time constants ranging from 1 to 30 s, particularly at positions V135 at the top of the ECD, P250 on the M2-M3 loop, and E243 on the top of the M2 α-helix (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Ion flux experiments show a decrease in channel activity when GLIC is pre-incubated with protons for more than 100 ms.
source: Second, ion flux experiments show a decrease in channel activity when GLIC is pre-incubated with protons for a more than 100 ms.
evidence: This is supported by thallium flux assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both GLIC Cys-less and mutant Bimane-136-W101 show fast fluorescence decay with a rate of ≈ 80 s−1 after incubation for 15 ms at pH 4.5 and 4.2.
source: Both GLIC Cys-less and mutant Bimane-136-W101 show fast fluorescence decay with a rate of ≈ 80 s−1 after incubation for 15 ms at pH 4.5 and 4.2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by thallium flux assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The fast fluorescence decay indicates robust activation of GLIC under acidic conditions.
source: This indicates robust activation of GLIC under these acidic conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the fast quenching rate in the thallium flux assay.

claim: The quenching kinetics at pH 4.5 and 4.2 are identical.
source: The quenching kinetics at both pH values are identical (Figure 7B), suggesting that activation is already maximal at pH 4.5.
evidence: This is supported by thallium flux assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Activation is already maximal at pH 4.5.
source: The quenching kinetics at both pH values are identical (Figure 7B), suggesting that activation is already maximal at pH 4.5.
evidence: This is inferred from the identical quenching kinetics at pH 4.5 and 4.2.

claim: Very slow kinetics (≈ 3 s−1) are observed after incubating the channels for 15 ms at pH 5.2.
source: In contrast, very slow kinetics (≈ 3 s−1) are observed after incubating the channels for 15 ms at pH 5.2 (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1) which indicates that these conditions lead to little channel activation.
evidence: This is supported by thallium flux assay data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: pH 5.2 conditions lead to little channel activation.
source: In contrast, very slow kinetics (≈ 3 s−1) are observed after incubating the channels for 15 ms at pH 5.2 (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1) which indicates that these conditions lead to little channel activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the slow quenching kinetics at pH 5.2.

claim: The pH50 for GLIC Cys-less is estimated at pH 4.6.
source: According to these data the pH50 for GLIC Cys-less and GLIC Bimane-136-W101 is estimated at pH 4.6 and pH 4.7, respectively (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by thallium flux assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The pH50 for GLIC Bimane-136-W101 is estimated at pH 4.7.
source: According to these data the pH50 for GLIC Cys-less and GLIC Bimane-136-W101 is estimated at pH 4.6 and pH 4.7, respectively (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by thallium flux assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: 15 ms are sufficient to reach the maximal activation of GLIC.
source: Increasing the pre-mix time did not increase the rates of fluorescence quenching at any of the pH values tested, suggesting that 15 ms are sufficient to reach the maximal activation of GLIC.
evidence: This is inferred from the thallium flux assay data showing no increase in quenching rate with longer pre-incubation times.

claim: Prolonged incubation (above 25 ms) at low pH reduced the rates of quenching, possibly reflecting GLIC desensitization in asolectin liposomes.
source: On the contrary, prolonged incubation (above 25 ms) at low pH reduced the rates of quenching, possibly reflecting GLIC desensitization in asolectin liposomes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by thallium flux assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1, with speculation about desensitization.

claim: For the Bimane-136-W101 mutant in asolectin liposomes, the pH-fluorescence relationship and the pH-ion flux relationship are separated by more than one order of magnitude.
source: For the Bimane-136-W101 mutant in asolectin liposomes, the pH-fluorescence relationship (∆F curves), which reports on protein motions, and the pH-ion flux relationship (∆If curves), which reports on activity, are separated by more than one order of magnitude (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of fluorescence and ion flux data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: At pH 5, the majority of the fluorescence changes are completed, whereas almost no receptors are yet active.
source: Indeed, at pH 5, the majority of the fluorescence changes are completed, whereas almost no receptors are yet active.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of fluorescence and ion flux data.

claim: The data directly reveal an intermediate conformation of the protein, where the quaternary motion of positions 136 and 101 moving closer together has occurred, but where the channel is still closed.
source: This directly reveals an intermediate conformation of the protein, where the quaternary motion of positions 136 and 101 moving closer together has occurred, but where the channel is still closed.
evidence: This is inferred from the separation between fluorescence and ion flux pH-response curves.

claim: Activation curves in oocytes (∆I curves) are significantly shifted to higher proton concentrations as compared to ∆F curves, especially at positions 135 and 250.
source: Interestingly, a similar scenario is seen at other positions, for which activation curves in oocytes (∆I curves) are significantly shifted to higher proton concentrations as compared to ∆F curves, especially at positions 135 and 250 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of electrophysiology and fluorescence data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The intermediate conformation involves global motions of the protein, notably the adjacent subunits moving closer at the level of the ECD (positions 136–101 and 135–72) as well as the separation between positions 250 and 197 and thus the outward motion of the M2-M3 loop.
source: Hence, our data suggest that the intermediate conformation involves global motions of the protein, notably the adjacent subunits moving closer at the level of the ECD (positions 136–101 and 135–72) as well as the separation between positions 250 and 197 and thus the outward motion of the M2-M3 loop.
evidence: This is inferred from the fluorescence data at multiple positions showing conformational changes before channel opening.

claim: Measurement of the variation of Cβ-Cβ distances between the pH 7 and pH 4 structures parallel the motions inferred from fluorescence measurements at positions 136–101, 133–103 and 33–160 in the ECD.
source: Interestingly, measurement of the variation of Cβ-Cβ distances between the pH 7 and pH 4 structures parallel the motions inferred from fluorescence measurements at positions 136–101, 133–103 and 33–160 in the ECD, that are reporting the subunits moving closer together, and positions 250–197 that follow the separation of the M2-M3 loop from the top of M1 (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data shown in Supplementary file 1B.

claim: The molecular reorganizations inferred from the comparison of the two X-ray structures are likely contributing to the ensemble motions followed by fluorescence.
source: It is thus likely that the molecular reorganizations inferred from the comparison of the two X-ray structures are contributing to the ensemble motions followed by fluorescence.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between structural changes and fluorescence data.

claim: At positions 243–238 and 136–178, no correlation between the structures and the population ensembles can be observed.
source: However, at other positions, namely at pairs 243–238 (top of the TMD) and 136–178 (Loop C), no correlation between the structures and the population ensembles can be observed.
evidence: This is based on comparison of structural and fluorescence data.

claim: At positions 243–238 and 136–178, the receptors might undergo different reorganizations when GLIC is outside of the crystal, and/or additional conformational states are contributing to the overall fluorescence signal.
source: This suggests that, at these levels, the receptors might undergo different reorganizations when GLIC is outside of the crystal, and/or that additional conformational states are contributing to the overall fluorescence signal.
evidence: This is speculated based on the lack of correlation between structural and fluorescence data at these positions.

claim: For GLIC reconstituted in asolectin liposomes recorded in the inside-out configuration, the activation time constant (τ) is in the 10 ms range upon activation by pH 2.5.
source: For GLIC reconstituted in asolectin liposomes recorded in the inside-out configuration, the activation time constant (τ) is in the 10 ms range upon activation by a very high proton concentration (pH 2.5) (Velisetty and Chakrapani, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Velisetty and Chakrapani, 2012.

claim: In HEK cells, out-side-out patch clamp recordings under fast perfusion, at pH 4, reveal activation time constants ranging from 30 to 150 ms.
source: Likewise, in HEK cells, out-side-out patch clamp recordings under fast perfusion, at pH 4, reveal activation time constants ranging from 30 to 150 ms (Laha et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Laha et al., 2013.

claim: The very fast transition toward the intermediate state is likely part of the activation mechanism.
source: While the activation kinetics of GLIC in liposomes could not be resolved in the present study, it is likely that the very fast transition toward the intermediate state is part of the activation mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data showing very fast conformational changes.

claim: A global 'pre-activation' step first occurs in under 2 ms, involving the whole ECD compaction and the outward motion of the M2-M3 loop, followed by a slower and more localized transition for channel opening.
source: Altogether, we propose a kinetic scheme where a global 'pre-activation' step first occurs in under 2 ms, involving the whole ECD compaction and the outward motion of the M2-M3 loop, followed by a slower and more localized transition for channel opening (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a proposed kinetic model based on the fluorescence and ion flux data.

claim: The slower transition for channel opening may be related to the fluorescence changes observed in the 5–966 ms ranges, particularly marked for the 243 reporter.
source: This latter motion may plausibly be related to the fluorescence changes observed in the 5–966 ms ranges, that are particularly marked for the 243 reporter which is located near the channel gate.
evidence: This is speculated based on the kinetic data at position 243.

claim: The structures of GLIC bearing a disulphide bridge C33-C245, as well as the single mutant GLIC E243P, show the M2-M3 loop revolved outwards, identically as for GLICpH 4, but still with a closed ion channel.
source: Among these, the structures of GLIC bearing a disulphide bridge C33-C245, as well as the single mutant GLIC E243P, show a particularity with the M2-M3 loop revolved outwards, identically as for GLICpH 4, but still with a closed ion channel.
evidence: This is based on structural data from previous studies.

claim: The locally-closed conformation with outward M2-M3 loop could be a candidate for the pre-active state of GLIC.
source: Hence, we may speculate that this particular LC conformation could be a candidate for the pre-active state of GLIC, since it shows compaction of the ECD and motion of the M2-M3 loop without channel opening.
evidence: This is speculated based on structural similarities to the proposed pre-active state.

claim: In HEK cells, out-side-out patch clamp recordings show desensitization to be biphasic, with a fast component observed on half of the patches (τ around 200 ms), followed by a slow component observed in all patches (τ around 10 s).
source: Indeed, in HEK cells, out-side-out patch clamp recordings show desensitization to be biphasic, with a fast component observed on half of the patches (τ around 200 ms), followed by a slow component observed in all patches (τ around 10 s) (Laha et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Laha et al., 2013.

claim: Previous analysis of the desensitization mechanism of GLIC by EPR supports the view that desensitization proceeds through a narrowing of the lower part of the channel.
source: Interestingly, previous analysis of the desensitization mechanism of GLIC by EPR (Velisetty and Chakrapani, 2012), and of other pLGICs by mutagenesis (Gielen et al., 2015) and NMR (Kinde et al., 2015), support the view that desensitization proceeds through a narrowing of the lower part of the channel.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Velisetty and Chakrapani, 2012; Gielen et al., 2015; Kinde et al., 2015.

claim: Recently published X-ray structures of a GABAA receptor and of the α4β2 nAChR were proposed to correspond to a desensitized conformation and show a channel constriction in the bottom part of the ECD.
source: Additionally, recently published X-ray structures of a GABAA receptor (Miller et al., 2014) and of the α4β2 nAChR (Morales-Perez et al., 2016) were proposed to correspond to a desensitized conformation and show a channel constriction in the bottom part of the ECD.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2014 and Morales-Perez et al., 2016.

claim: Desensitization might occur through reorganizations in the TMD, with comparatively smaller motion at the ECD and particularly at the ECD-TMD interface.
source: Therefore, desensitization might occur through reorganizations in the TMD, with comparatively smaller motion at the ECD and particularly at the ECD-TMD interface.
evidence: This is inferred from structural and functional data on desensitization.

claim: Available structures of eukaryotic pLGICs suggest a quaternary compaction of the ECD upon agonist binding.
source: Interestingly, available structures of eukaryotic pLGICs, namely the GluClαR (Hibbs and Gouaux, 2011; Althoff et al., 2014) and the α1GlyR (Du et al., 2015), also suggest a quaternary compaction of the ECD upon agonist binding, as well as outward motions of the M2-M3 loop upon channel opening that are similar to that observed on GLIC.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hibbs and Gouaux, 2011; Althoff et al., 2014; Du et al., 2015.

claim: Available structures of eukaryotic pLGICs suggest outward motions of the M2-M3 loop upon channel opening that are similar to that observed on GLIC.
source: Interestingly, available structures of eukaryotic pLGICs, namely the GluClαR (Hibbs and Gouaux, 2011; Althoff et al., 2014) and the α1GlyR (Du et al., 2015), also suggest a quaternary compaction of the ECD upon agonist binding, as well as outward motions of the M2-M3 loop upon channel opening that are similar to that observed on GLIC.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hibbs and Gouaux, 2011; Althoff et al., 2014; Du et al., 2015.

claim: ϕ-value analysis following extensive mutational analysis of the muscle nAChR suggests that the top of the ECD around the orthosteric pocket, as well as the M2-M3 loop move early in the course of the gating transition toward the active state.
source: In addition, ϕ-value analysis following extensive mutational analysis of the muscle nAChR further suggest that the top of the ECD around the orthosteric pocket, as well as the M2-M3 loop move early in the course of the gating transition toward the active state (Purohit et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Purohit et al., 2013.

claim: The study provides a structural template to investigate the gating of eukaryotic and mammalian receptors.
source: The present study thus not only sheds light on the gating mechanism of the pLGIC model GLIC, but also provides a structural template to investigate the gating of eukaryotic and mammalian receptors.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the broader implications of the study.

claim: The monobromo bimane (mBBr) does not efficiently label surface receptors in Xenopus oocytes.
source: Indeed, we found that the currently used mBBr (Monobromo bimane) does not efficiently label surface receptors, since the reporter mutant GLIC Q193C (pre-M1), which is fully inhibited by reaction with methyl-methanethiosulfate (MMTS) (Figure 2B), is neither affected nor protected from MMTS inhibition by mBBr treatment.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Control experiments on CHO cells expressing GLIC-D136C showed no surface labeling with mBBr, but clear accumulation of the fluorophore in the cytoplasm.
source: Control experiments on chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells expressing GLIC-D136C showed no surface labeling, but clear accumulation of the fluorophore in the cytoplasm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The bimane-derived Bunte salt (BBs) was synthesized to decrease the hydrophobicity of the reagent.
source: To decrease the hydrophobicity of the reagent, we synthesized the bimane-derived Bunte salt (BBs), introducing a negatively charged SO3− leaving group (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a description of the chemical synthesis performed in the study.

claim: After reaction with cysteine residues, the mBBr and BBs yield almost the same coupling product, with similar fluorescence and side-chain volume.
source: After reaction with cysteine residues, the mBBr and BBs yield almost the same coupling product, with similar fluorescence and side-chain volume (Mansoor and Farrens, 2004) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mansoor and Farrens, 2004 and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GLIC-expressing CHO cells show weak entry of the BBs in the cytoplasm and strong labeling at the membrane.
source: GLIC-expressing CHO cells show weak entry of the BBs in the cytoplasm and strong labeling at the membrane (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: BBs labeling of Q193C-expressing oocytes led to a severe loss of function indicating an efficient reaction with the surface receptors.
source: Accordingly, BBs labeling of Q193C-expressing oocytes led to a severe loss of function indicating an efficient reaction with the surface receptors (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: After BBs labeling, currents showed wild-type like biphasic GLIC activation kinetics, with time constants ranging from 1 to 2.8 s (τ1) and 5 to 8.9 s (τ2).
source: For all functional mutants, after BBs labeling, currents showed wild-type like biphasic GLIC activation kinetics, with time constants ranging from 1 to 2.8 s (τ1) and 5 to 8.9 s (τ2) (Table 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Table 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: P250C bearing its endogenous quencher Y197 displays slower kinetics of activation (5.4 s and 50 s).
source: except for P250C baring its endogenous quencher Y197 (termed P250C-Y197) which displays slower kinetics of activation (5.4 s and 50 s).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Table 2.

claim: pH-current relationship measurements show ∆pH50 of less than one between wild-type and BBs-labeled mutants.
source: pH-current relationship measurements show ∆pH50 (pH value for which half of the maximal electrophysiological response is recorded) of less than one between wild-type and BBs-labeled mutants (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Table 1.

claim: The labeling with the small BBs probe weakly affects the gating in most cases.
source: Thus, the labeling with the small BBs probe weakly affects the gating in most cases.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiology data showing minimal changes in pH50 and activation kinetics after labeling.

claim: W72 is a residue strictly conserved in all pLGICs.
source: W72 is a residue strictly conserved in all pLGICs (Corringer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Corringer et al., 2012.
